title: OpenAI Prompting in Practice
summary: This intermediate module teaches you to turn a vague request into a clear, structured prompt for OpenAI systems. After completing it, you can specify a goal, provide relevant context, state constraints, request an output format, and improve a prompt through controlled revision.
objectives: Rewrite an ambiguous request as a prompt with a specific goal, relevant context, and explicit constraints.
Request an output format that makes a response easier to evaluate and use.
Separate instructions from supporting material so their roles are clear.
Revise one prompt element at a time and compare the resulting responses against stated criteria.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you have already entered basic prompts and read the resulting responses, but it does not assume knowledge of programming, model internals, or provider configuration.

Before this module, you may be able to ask for a response without making the success criteria explicit. After this module, you can construct and revise a prompt whose goal, context, constraints, and expected output are clear enough to evaluate.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The prior cited source was content/modules/openai-practice/openai-prompting-in-practice.json, which was identified as having an unregistered publisher and as never having been verified. This update replaces that citation with OpenAI's official Prompt engineering guide at the HTTPS address listed in the sources field.

The change affects source attribution, verification metadata, and the support for the prompting recommendations in this module. The practical focus remains constructing clear prompts, separating supporting material, specifying the desired output, and revising prompts systematically.

sections.title: Build a clear request
paragraphs: Begin with the task the response must perform. Replace broad instructions such as "Help me with this report" with an observable goal such as "Summarize the report for a reader who has not seen it." A concrete goal gives you a direct basis for deciding whether the response succeeded.

Add only the context needed to perform that task. Useful context can identify the intended audience, the purpose of the response, definitions that matter, or source material that must be used. Context should inform the task rather than hide it.

State constraints explicitly when they matter. A constraint can limit scope, establish tone, identify information that must be included, or prohibit unsupported additions. Do not rely on the system to infer a requirement that you can state directly.
sections.callout: A practical prompt can be organized as goal, context, constraints, and output format. Not every request needs all four parts, but each omitted part should be omitted deliberately.

sections.title: Separate instructions from supporting material
paragraphs: When a prompt includes text to summarize, classify, transform, or analyze, distinguish that material from the instructions. Clear labels or delimiters help show where the task description ends and the supporting material begins.

For example, a prompt can first state the instruction, then label a passage as source text, and finally state what the response must contain. This structure is especially useful when the source text contains sentences that resemble instructions but are only material to be analyzed.
The separation does not guarantee a correct response. It makes the intended roles of the prompt's parts clearer and gives you a more precise structure to inspect when revising the request.

sections.title: Specify the output you need
paragraphs: Describe the shape of a useful response. You can request a short paragraph, a table with named columns, a numbered procedure, or another explicit structure. Include required fields or ordering when downstream use depends on them.

Match the requested format to the task. A table can help compare repeated attributes, while a short paragraph can be more suitable for a concise explanation. Avoid adding formatting requirements that do not help you judge or use the result.

If style matters, describe it in concrete terms connected to the audience and purpose. For example, ask for plain language for a non-specialist reader rather than relying only on a vague instruction to make the response better.

sections.title: Use examples when description is not enough
paragraphs: An example can demonstrate a pattern that is difficult to express as a rule. A useful example pairs a representative input with the kind of output you want, while remaining consistent with the written instructions.

Examples should clarify the task rather than replace its definition. If an example conflicts with an instruction, revise the prompt so both communicate the same requirement. Use examples that represent the behavior you actually want repeated.
Do not assume that one example covers every case. Evaluate the resulting prompt with more than one relevant input, especially when the inputs can vary in length, wording, or subject.

sections.title: Revise systematically
paragraphs: Prompt improvement is easier to evaluate when you change one meaningful element at a time. You might first clarify the goal, then add missing context, then tighten a constraint, and finally refine the output format. If you change everything at once, it becomes harder to identify which revision helped.

Before comparing responses, write down the criteria that matter. Criteria can include factual grounding in supplied material, inclusion of required points, adherence to scope, suitability for the audience, and compliance with the requested format.

Keep the input and evaluation criteria stable while comparing prompt revisions. Select a revision because it performs better against those criteria, not merely because its response is longer or sounds more confident.
sections.callout: A longer prompt is not automatically a better prompt. Include details that define the task or help evaluate success, and remove details that create ambiguity or conflict.

sections.title: Worked revision
paragraphs: Consider the vague request "Summarize this." It does not identify the audience, purpose, source boundaries, required coverage, or response format.

A clearer revision is: "Summarize the source text for a non-specialist reader. Explain the main conclusion and two supporting points. Use only information in the labeled source text. Return one paragraph followed by two numbered points." The revision supplies an audience, required content, a grounding constraint, and an output structure.

You can evaluate the revised response by checking four questions: Is the main conclusion present? Are there exactly two supporting points? Does every claim come from the source text? Does the response follow the requested paragraph and numbered-point structure? These checks turn a subjective impression into explicit criteria.

questions.prompt: Which revision most clearly defines an observable goal?
choices: Make this much better.
Summarize the source text for a reader who has not seen it, including the main conclusion and two supporting points.
Think carefully about the text.
Write whatever seems useful.
questions.explanation: The correct choice names the task, audience, and required content. The other choices do not provide clear success criteria.

questions.prompt: Why should instructions be separated from source material in a prompt?
choices: To make the intended role of each part clearer.
To guarantee that every response is correct.
To remove the need for a task instruction.
To make every prompt longer.
questions.explanation: The module explains that labels or delimiters clarify where instructions end and supporting material begins. It also states that this separation does not guarantee correctness.

questions.prompt: When is an explicit output format most useful?
choices: When the structure helps you evaluate or use the response.
Whenever it makes the prompt contain more words.
Only when no source material is provided.
When you want to avoid stating the task.
questions.explanation: The module recommends requesting a format that supports evaluation or downstream use, rather than adding structure that serves no purpose.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended way to compare prompt revisions?
choices: Change several unrelated elements and select the longest response.
Change one meaningful element at a time while keeping the input and evaluation criteria stable.
Choose the response that sounds most confident without checking it.
Remove the success criteria before making a comparison.
questions.explanation: Changing one meaningful element at a time and keeping the comparison conditions stable makes it easier to identify which revision affected the result.

questions.prompt: What source change does this update record?
choices: An unverified local citation was replaced with OpenAI's official Prompt engineering guide.
The module added a prerequisite from another catalogue entry.
The module adopted a new configuration key.
The module replaced OpenAI with a provider-neutral subject.
